what_its_for: Lisinopril is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension), heart failure, and to protect your kidneys if you have diabetes. Lowering high blood pressure helps prevent strokes, heart attacks, and kidney problems. It belongs to a group of medicines called ACE inhibitors.
how_to_take: Take lisinopril by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember. If you are using the liquid form (Qbrelis), use the measuring device provided — never use a regular kitchen spoon.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition. Doses typically start low and may be gradually increased. Common starting doses range from 5 mg to 10 mg once daily, and the usual maintenance dose is between 10 mg and 40 mg once daily. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store lisinopril tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. If you have the liquid form, check the label for specific storage instructions, as it may need to be refrigerated.
what_to_avoid: Avoid using salt substitutes or low-sodium products that contain potassium, as this can raise your potassium levels to a dangerous range. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can further lower your blood pressure and make you feel dizzy or faint. Be careful when standing up quickly, especially in hot weather or after exercise, as this medicine can cause dizziness. Do not take anti-inflammatory pain relievers like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve) without first checking with your doctor, as they can reduce how well lisinopril works and harm your kidneys.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (this could be a serious allergic reaction called angioedema); difficulty breathing or swallowing; a sudden or severe drop in blood pressure causing fainting; signs of high potassium such as muscle weakness, irregular heartbeat, or numbness and tingling; signs of kidney problems such as decreased urination or swelling in your legs; or if you become pregnant, since lisinopril can seriously harm an unborn baby. Also contact your doctor if you develop a persistent dry cough, which is a common side effect of this medication.
when_it_works: Lisinopril begins lowering your blood pressure within a few hours of your first dose. However, it may take 2 to 4 weeks of regular use to see the full benefit. Even if you feel fine, keep taking it every day — high blood pressure usually has no symptoms, and this medicine works best when taken consistently as prescribed.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do NOT take lisinopril if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby, especially during the second and third trimesters. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant while taking this medicine. Breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding, as it is not known whether lisinopril passes into breast milk. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to the blood-pressure-lowering effects and may be at higher risk for dizziness and falls. Start low and go slow. Kidney disease: Your dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney problems. Your doctor will monitor your kidney function and potassium levels with regular blood tests. Children: Lisinopril can be used in children 6 years and older for high blood pressure, but it should not be used in children with certain kidney conditions. The dose is based on the child's weight.
